title: The Jade King
tagline: He ruled Palenque 68 years and inscribed eternity in stone.

scenes.text: Palenque, 615 CE. K'inich Janaab' Pakal I ascends to the throne at age 12. He will reign for 68 years — longer than any other documented ruler in the Americas.
He begins rebuilding a kingdom that has suffered military defeats. His mother served as regent for years; he inherits instability and turns it into a golden age.

challenge.instruction: Lakamha', the city of big water, needs its gardens fed. Open the sluices so water runs down the terraces to every garden — and keep the flood out of the young king's town.
challenge.fact: Pakal became king of Palenque at age 12 in 615 CE and ruled until his death in 683 CE — 68 years on the throne, the longest reign in all of pre-Columbian history. Under his rule, Palenque transformed from a minor city into one of the most powerful and artistically sophisticated kingdoms of the Classic Maya world.

scenes.text: The Temple of the Inscriptions: a nine-level pyramid encoding his life, his lineage, and the Maya concept of cyclical time. It will serve as his tomb — discovered sealed for 1,300 years.

challenge.instruction: The nine terraces of the Temple of the Inscriptions rise stone by stone. Haul each block onto its mark — once a stone is set it cannot be moved again, so raise them in the right order.
challenge.fact: The Temple of the Inscriptions stood in plain sight for centuries — one of Palenque's most prominent structures. But its tomb was not discovered until 1952, when Mexican archaeologist Alberto Ruz Lhuillier noticed a stone floor with plugged holes and spent four years clearing a rubble-filled staircase before reaching Pakal's burial chamber 25 metres below.

params.title: The Temple of the Inscriptions
params.intro: Once a limestone block drops onto its terrace mark it is set for good — it can never be pushed off again, or rolled across another mark. Raise the stones in the right order.

scenes.text: The Palenque Palace — a vast complex with a four-story tower unique in Classic Maya architecture. Astronomers used it to track Venus, eclipses, and the movement of the sun.

challenge.instruction: The Palace astronomers read the sun to time the planting. Plan the milpas year by year so Palenque has maize and beans — and let the tired fields lie fallow.
challenge.fact: The sarcophagus lid of Pakal's tomb shows him at the moment of death, descending into the Maya underworld (Xibalba) on the World Tree. For decades Western scholars misread the image as an astronaut in a spacecraft — a famous case of wishful thinking overriding careful analysis. Maya specialists recognized it as a standard resurrection narrative immediately.

scenes.text: The Maya Long Count calendar inscribed at Palenque reaches back 4 billion years — evidence of cosmological thinking that dwarfs contemporary European astronomy.

challenge.instruction: Descend the hidden stairway beneath the Temple of the Inscriptions, sealed with rubble for 1,300 years, to the jade king's chamber at the pyramid's heart.
challenge.fact: The staircase descending to Pakal's tomb is 25 metres long and was completely filled with rubble when Alberto Ruz first entered. His team spent four excavation seasons (1949–1952) removing it stone by stone. When they finally broke through the sealed chamber door, they found a jade-encrusted sarcophagus surrounded by six sacrificed retainers and walls painted with the nine lords of the Maya underworld.

scenes.text: When Alberto Ruz Lhuillier unsealed Pakal's tomb in 1952, he found jade mosaic mask, jade jewelry, red cinnabar — a king preserved in jade for eternity. History confirmed mythology.

challenge.instruction: Deep under the temple, Ruz Lhuillier's crew faces the carved stone lid of Pakal's sarcophagus. Set the fulcrum and the bar so the men can raise the slab high enough to look inside.
challenge.fact: The carved limestone lid of Pakal's sarcophagus measures about 3.8 by 2.2 metres and weighs several tonnes. In November 1952 Ruz's team raised it with jacks and wedged logs beneath it, and saw the king in his jade mask.

challenge.instruction: Pakal's builders tied his tomb to the sky. Find the low winter sun's angle from the shadow it casts across the Palace plaza.
challenge.fact: Maya builders worked without metal tools or draft animals, yet set their monuments to the sky. Linda Schele noted in the 1970s that, seen from the Palace, the sun at the winter solstice sets directly behind the Temple of the Inscriptions — as if the dying sun were entering Pakal's tomb.

params.title: The Solstice Sun at Palenque
params.goal: Drag the setting sun until the 2 m stela casts a shadow exactly 10 m long. Only the sun's angle above the horizon is shown.
params.explanation: tan θ = 2/10 → θ ≈ 11.3°. Maya astronomers followed the sun's path through the year; seen from the Palace at Palenque, the winter-solstice sun sets behind the Temple of the Inscriptions.

scenes.speaker: Pakal the Great
scenes.text: Taira no Tadanori waits at Changan, but nothing is happening there, and without an event there is no fight. I will go first; the turn after I arrive, play the Coup card on Changan and we attack.

challenge.instruction: Fight lesson 3 · Starting an Event. Deploy Pakal the Great to Changan and End Turn. Next turn play the Coup card there, add your follower and win one attack.
challenge.fact: Event cards start a scenario at a location where you already have a Great Person, and only one who arrived on an earlier turn can start it. A local event keeps running until a player ends it.
